summary: Add end-to-end tests for wp-admin screens
_description:
#49507 adds e2e tests for the edit posts page. The goal is to write tests for all the admin, but we should be clear on which parts need most testing and what exactly to test. To kick things off, I'm making a list of all the pages, some of the tests we should write, and some questions that occurred to me. Feedback on what to add, change or remove is very welcome!

Dashboard:
* Quick draft section: add title, save draft, navigate to posts page and check it's there.

Updates page: not sure how we should test this one.

Categories:
* Add new category: add name, click add new category button, check if it appears in list
* Check that bulk deleting all categories leaves “uncategorized” untouched
* Add child category
* Delete category
* Search for category
* Search for non-existing category

Tags: same as categories.

Media:
* Add image to library
* Edit image alt text, title, desc
* Search for image
* Search for non-existing image

Pages: same as posts (see #49507)

Comments:
* Create post, view it, add a comment, check that it displays in comments page.

Themes:
* Search for a theme
* Activate a theme
* Delete a theme, then search for it
* Add new theme and activate it

Customize: this is pretty theme-dependent, so we should pick a theme and check a few flows on it.

Widgets and Menus: might not be worth writing tests yet as these screens are being re-written.

Theme editor:
* Add a line of CSS in the theme stylesheet and check for it in the front end?

Plugins: how should we test this page?

Users:
* Add new user
* Search for user 
* change user role
* Check admin user can't change itself to subscriber

Profile: there are lots of options here, should we test changes to each of them? Some may not be relevant, e.g. profile pic just takes us to Gravatar.

Import: We could test whether the plugins install correctly, but any further than that should be unnecessary (the plugins should have their own tests)

Export/Export personal data: would it be worth trying to check the contents of the downloaded files? 

Site health: there's no real interaction on this page, so maybe we can skip it.

Erase personal data: not sure how to test this one.

Settings: like profile, lots of options here. Test each individually?

summary: render_block_core_template_part / get_404_template is called when in any admin area
_description:
it seems that no matter where you are in the admin area, render_block_core_template_part is invoked. I have no idea why this would be required when in the reading settings area, for example.

to replicate:
1. add error log to render_block_core_template_part like so:

{{{#!php

<?php
/**
 * Server-side rendering of the `core/template-part` block.
 *
 * @package WordPress
 */

/**
 * Renders the `core/template-part` block on the server.
 *
 * @since 5.9.0
 *
 * @global WP_Embed $wp_embed WordPress Embed object.
 *
 * @param array $attributes The block attributes.
 *
 * @return string The render.
 */
function render_block_core_template_part( $attributes ) {
	static $seen_ids = array();

	error_log('WHY IS THIS RENDERING ' . print_r($attributes, true));
	$template_part_id = null;
	$content          = null;
...
}}}

2. check error log, observe that header and footer template parts are there.

This is on the 2025 theme, with no other plugins installed.

Digging deeper:
It appears that in template-loader.php, when on any admin area, get_404_template is invoked... because is_404 is true, because the main query sees {{{$query_vars['p']}}} is empty, because we're not viewing a post.

So a bit more involved than I originally thought.

UPDATE: this was due to the site i was working on missing the file for the site favicon. in fetching the missing favicon, it was rendering the 404 template somewhere else. 

it's still rendering though, and it appears to be a browser plugin request. Using React Developer Tools extension attempts to look for /wp-admin/installHook.js.map, which doesn't exist, triggering the rendering of the 404 page template.

background: a block i'm working on does some complicated stuff, so I was looking to implement a simple caching / transient system to store the rendered output. This entails having a way to flush the cache - but while I was testing it in a custom admin area, there was one block transient that just wouldn't go away. as it turns out, that block was in the header template, and because of my missing favicon image, was getting invoked every time the admin area loaded, and then re-caching the block as it rendered a 404 for the favicon request. neat!

tldr: feels like 404 page templates shouldn't be rendered for requests like these, seems like a lot of extra stuff going on that doesn't need to be.

summary: Update counts in the folded admin menu don't refresh after updating a plugin
_description:
When the admin menu is folded, the update count next to "Plugins" doesn't change after you update a plugin on the page. It keeps the old number until you reload.

The admin menu prints each top-level item's update count twice: once in the menu link, and once in the submenu header (`.wp-submenu-head`). The submenu header is what shows when the menu is folded, either after clicking "Collapse Menu" or automatically on screens between 783 and 960 pixels wide. `wp.updates.refreshCount()` only updates the copy in the menu link, so the folded menu never changes.

=== Steps to reproduce
1. Have two plugins with updates available.
2. Make the browser window about 900 pixels wide, or click "Collapse Menu".
3. Go to "Plugins > Installed Plugins" and click "update now" for one of them.
4. Hover over "Plugins" in the admin menu.

Expected: the count shows 1.

Actual: it still shows 2. After updating both plugins it still shows 2 instead of no count.

The same thing happens with the "Themes" count in the network admin, which is also a top-level menu item. On a single site the theme count is on the "Themes" submenu item, so it isn't affected.

=== Environment
- WordPress: 7.2-alpha (trunk)
- Browser: Chromium 149
- Single site and multisite

I have a patch ready and will link the PR here.

summary: Revisions endpoint returns meta that isn't revisioned, so restoring a revision in the editor overwrites it
_description:
Hey there! I'm report that the block editor's Visual Revisions, new in 7.0, restores a revision by reading it from the REST API and saving its `title`, `excerpt`, `content` and `meta` onto the post. The `meta` part is where it goes wrong.

`WP_REST_Revisions_Controller` returns every `show_in_rest` meta key registered for the parent post type, read from the revision ID. Only keys with `revisions_enabled`, or added with the `wp_post_revision_meta_keys` filter, are ever stored on a revision, so the rest come back as their default, or `null` when the default doesn't pass the key's schema. The editor then saves those over the post's real values.

Patterns hit this right away, since `wp_pattern_sync_status` isn't revisioned and only allows `partial` or `unsynced`:

 * Restoring an unsynced pattern sends `null`, which deletes the status, so the pattern quietly becomes synced.
 * Restoring a synced pattern fails with a 500: "The wp_pattern_sync_status property has an invalid stored value, and cannot be updated to null." The content is already saved by then, so the restore half works and the user sees an error.

On other post types it's silent. Restoring resets every non-revisioned `show_in_rest` key: strings become `''`, keys with a registered `default` get that default, and multi keys are deleted.

The classic revisions screen is fine, because `wp_restore_post_revision()` only restores the keys from `wp_post_revision_meta_keys()`.

This was reported in Gutenberg as [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/84809 #84809], and @davidsword traced it to this endpoint. The editor can't tell which keys are revisioned, since `revisions_enabled` isn't exposed over REST, so the fix needs to happen here.

=== Steps to reproduce

 1. Register a meta key that isn't revisioned, for example in an mu-plugin:
{{{#!php
<?php
add_action( 'init', function () {
	register_post_meta( 'post', 'kept_meta', array(
		'show_in_rest' => true,
		'single'       => true,
		'type'         => 'string',
	) );
} );
}}}
 2. Create a post and update it a couple of times so it has revisions.
 3. Give it a value with `wp post meta update <ID> kept_meta hello`.
 4. With "Custom fields" turned off in the editor Preferences, so the editor uses Visual Revisions, open Revisions, move to an earlier revision, and click "Restore".
 5. `kept_meta` is now empty.

`GET /wp/v2/posts/<ID>/revisions/<revision ID>?context=edit` shows `"kept_meta": ""` even though nothing is stored on the revision. The steps for patterns are in the Gutenberg issue.

=== Proposed fix

Have the revisions endpoint only return, and only describe in its schema, the meta keys from `wp_post_revision_meta_keys()` for the parent post type. That matches what's stored on a revision and what the classic restore does, and the editor doesn't need a change. Autosave responses are built by the revisions controller, so they'd follow too, and autosaves only store revisioned keys anyway.

I have a patch with tests and will link the PR here.

summary: Add a plugin compatibility testing workflow to catch fatals with popular plugins before release
_description:
''Claude drafted this ticket, prompted and edited by me:''

WordPress 7.1 shipped and sites running WP Rocket began fataling on every request - `Uncaught TypeError: substr(): Argument #1 ($string) must be of type string, int given in Cloudflare.php:562`. Austin Ginder reported all of his customer sites went offline until he manually patched the plugin: https://x.com/austinginder/status/2090199834787541074

Core's CI is thorough about testing core itself - PHPUnit, e2e, install and upgrade paths - but nothing currently checks that a new version of WordPress can boot with popular plugins active. That check happens informally through beta testers, hosts, and plugin authors, and this incident shows the gap: a fatal on every request, on a top-tier plugin, made it through a full release cycle.

== Proposed approach ==

Add a GitHub Actions workflow (following the structure of the existing Installation Tests and Upgrade Tests workflows) that:

 * Fetches the current top 100 plugins by popularity from the WordPress.org plugins API at run time, so there is no hardcoded list to go stale.
 * Installs WordPress via WP-CLI at the version under test (`latest`, `nightly`, or a specific version, selectable via `workflow_dispatch` so release leads can point it at a beta or RC).
 * Installs and activates each plugin one at a time, in isolation, and verifies WordPress still runs: activation exit code, a WP-CLI load check, and front end / admin requests asserting no 5xx responses and no fatals in the debug log.
 * Reports a per-plugin pass/fail table in the workflow summary, tests all plugins even when one fails, and fails the run if any plugin fatals.
 * Runs weekly against nightly on a schedule, plus on demand.

To start this would be signal-only (scheduled and manual runs with Slack notifications on failure) rather than blocking - a broken third-party plugin should not turn core CI red on every commit.

Worth noting the limits honestly: the .org API only covers free directory plugins, so this exact incident (WP Rocket is a premium plugin) would not have been caught directly - but the same class of type-change fatal could just as easily land in any of the free plugins with millions of installs, and activation smoke testing is exactly where it would surface. Testing plugins in combination, premium plugin zips, and multisite are possible follow-ups.

Full acceptance criteria and an implementation plan are written up here: https://github.com/adamsilverstein/wordpress-develop/issues/64

Patch incoming (draft PR being prepared, will link it here once it is up).

What do others think - is a run of the top 100 the right starting scope, and does any of this overlap with existing plugin directory infrastructure?

== AI Use ==

Description written with Claude Code; the linked PR contains Claude-written code and says so in its own AI Use section. I will review and test.

summary: Media: Sideload and clean up the web-safe companion of a transcoded video upload
_description:
Follow up to #65549 (animated GIF video companions) and #64915 (source-format originals).

The client-side media flow in Gutenberg can now transcode an uploaded video that is not already web-safe (a `.mov` or `.mkv` container, a non-web-safe codec, an oversized frame or a high bitrate) to MP4/H.264 or WebM/VP9 in the browser. See https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/79375. The original upload is kept as the attachment, the same principle behind the `-scaled` image and the HEIC original, and the transcoded version is sideloaded as a companion file of that attachment. The `core/video` block points its playback `src` at the companion.

Core needs the server side of that flow:

 * Accept a video attachment as the sideload parent for a new `optimized_video` companion size. This is scoped to that one size; every other size still requires an image or PDF parent, since a video has no sub-sizes.
 * Record the companion under the `optimized_video` attachment metadata key on finalize, and treat it as a name the request is allowed to store.
 * Delete the companion alongside the attachment in `wp_delete_attachment_files()`, the way the `animated_video` companions are handled.
 * Expose a `wp_video_transcoding_keep_original` filter (default `true`) on the REST API index as `video_keep_original`, and preload it with the other media processing settings. When a site returns `false`, the editor transcodes before upload so only the optimized file is stored, trading the ability to download or regenerate from the original for lower storage use.

Patch incoming: https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13323

summary: Add core support for random content redirects
_description: WordPress Core does not include functionality to redirect a request to a randomly selected post or page. This behavior is currently implemented through plugins or custom code. This ticket proposes discussing whether a minimal, opt-in core implementation should exist. Any implementation could rely on existing query and rewrite APIs without introducing user-facing settings or defaults. @matt recently mentioned this as something to consider for 7.0 based on his early plugin here: https://wordpress.org/plugins/random-redirect/

summary: Script Loader: Add an API for stylesheet LINK tags
_description:
Stylesheet `<link>` tags in WordPress Core are largely built as HTML strings, so adding attributes such as a CSP `nonce`, `integrity`, or `crossorigin` often requires modifying markup through `style_loader_tag`. Scripts already have `wp_get_script_tag()` and the `wp_script_attributes` filter, while #51325 proposes the corresponding API for inline `<style>` tags.

The proposed API introduces `wp_get_style_link_tag()`, `wp_print_style_link_tag()`, and the `wp_style_attributes` filter, using `WP_HTML_Tag_Processor` to validate and escape attributes.

The implementation is split into three PRs:

* [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14498 PR #14498]: Adds the API and uses it in `WP_Styles::do_item()`, including right-to-left and alternate stylesheets, `wp_admin_css()`, and `locale_stylesheet()`.
* [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14499 PR #14499]: Updates the remaining Core call sites in `wp_ajax_parse_embed()`, `wp_ajax_parse_media_shortcode()`, and the deprecated theme compatibility header.
* [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14500 PR #14500]: Updates Twenty Ten and Twenty Eleven, with a fallback for older WordPress versions.

PRs #14499 and #14500 depend on #14498.

== Backward compatibility ==

The existing `style_loader_tag` and `wp_admin_css` filters remain available. Unlike the changes to script tags in [56687], the historical quoting, escaping, and attribute order are preserved for existing attributes that `wp_style_attributes` does not modify. The new attributes filter runs before the legacy filters.

The filter cannot change or remove an existing `id`, since other code may depend on it. `style_loader_tag` also continues to receive the original escaped URL, even if `wp_style_attributes` modifies `href`.

One compatibility change is that `WP_Styles::do_item()` now uses `get_src()` instead of `_css_href()`, so subclasses overriding `_css_href()` no longer affect the printed URL.

Additionally, stylesheet URLs previously printed without escaping by `locale_stylesheet()` and the remaining Core call sites in PR #14499 are now escaped.

summary: AI Client lacks filters for customizing model selection and generation parameters
_description:
The AI Client in WordPress 7.0 provides very limited filtering capabilities for third-party plugin customization.

== Existing Filters ==

Currently, only two filters exist:

* `wp_ai_client_default_request_timeout` (HTTP timeout only)
* `wp_ai_client_prevent_prompt` (request abort only)

== Current Limitations ==

There is currently **no way** for third-party plugins to customize:

* Model selection per-capability (text generation, image generation, vision)
* Generation parameters:
  * `temperature`
  * `max_tokens`
  * `top_p`
  * `top_k`
  * `presence_penalty`
  * `frequency_penalty`
* The PSR-14 `BeforeGenerateResultEvent` is read-only and cannot modify parameters

== Impact ==

This severely limits the ability of plugin developers to build AI-powered features with custom behavior and control. Plugin developers cannot:

* Dynamically select different models based on context or user role
* Adjust temperature for deterministic vs. creative output
* Control token limits per-capability or per-context
* Set request timeouts per-capability
* Conditionally modify generation parameters based on post type, user subscription, or other factors

== Why This Matters ==

Without these hooks, developers are forced to use workarounds and cannot leverage standard WordPress filter conventions for AI Client customization. This limits the extensibility of the AI Client and prevents a rich ecosystem of AI-powered plugins from being built.

summary: wp_should_load_block_assets_on_demand doing it wrong too early
_description:
`wp_should_load_block_assets_on_demand()` calls `wp_is_rest_endpoint()` which generally only works after `parse_request` hook (since that's where the constant gets defined) https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/script-loader.php#L2644 since it will always return false before that hook.

The same thing also for `wp_should_load_separate_core_block_assets()`  https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/script-loader.php#L2609

However it's often called way too early, e.g. on "init" hook, e.g. in WooCommerce https://github.com/woocommerce/woocommerce/blob/trunk/plugins/woocommerce/src/Blocks/BlockTypesController.php#L632 and https://github.com/woocommerce/woocommerce/blob/trunk/plugins/woocommerce/src/Blocks/BlockTypesController.php#L633

Or in WP core itself, e.g. when calling `wp_register_style(` on "init", it will subsequently call `wp_default_styles()` and then the load block assets on demand function.
The same also in WP core `register_block_type_from_metadata(`, essentially all the stuff on init in "blocks" wp-includes, e.g. `register_block_core_archives()` on init
Or for example even in the file that's declaring those: https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/script-loader.php#L1798

I guess that all those "init" registered block things should be moved to run later on "parse_request" (or "wp") hook? Or alternatively, remove the "wp_is_rest_endpoint()" check since at the point in time it's called on "init", it's not ready yet and always returns false.

Possibly add a "doing_it_wrong" in wp_is_serving_rest_request for ! did_action( 'parse_request' )

summary: Themes: Clarify the difference between 'editor-style' and 'editor-styles' theme support
_description:
`add_editor_style()`, `remove_editor_styles()` and `remove_theme_support()` use the theme support feature {{{editor-style}}} (singular), while the block editor uses {{{editor-styles}}} (plural). This looks like a typo, but they are two separate features:

 * {{{editor-style}}} (since 3.0) is an internal marker set by {{{add_editor_style()}}} for the TinyMCE stylesheets.
 * {{{editor-styles}}} (since 5.0) is the theme's opt-in that lets the block editor load the stylesheets registered with {{{add_editor_style()}}}. Block themes get it by default.

Renaming one to the other would break backward compatibility (see comment:14 and comment:16). The goal of this ticket is to document the distinction inline, so the names are no longer mistaken for a typo.

Docs: https://developer.wordpress.org/block-editor/how-to-guides/themes/theme-support/#editor-styles

=== Original description ===

In the functions `add_editor_style()`, `remove_editor_styles()` and `remove_theme_support()` the Theme `$feature` parameter`editor-style` is used instead of `editor-styles`.

It should be: `add_theme_support( 'editor-styles' );`

See docs: https://developer.wordpress.org/block-editor/how-to-guides/themes/theme-support/#editor-styles
See code docs: https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/8d0aed455b1790c5d51386f7675d9e8d68e48edf/src/wp-includes/theme.php#L2672

summary: Application password UX improvements
_description:
This ticket covers several related UX improvements for the application password approval screen.

These apply to the screen at `wp-admin/authorize-application.php` and its various URL query parameters.

1. Increase clarity about the target URL that will receive credentials if the request is approved. The only aspect of this URL that the user should be concerned about is its host name, and it should be front and centre.
2. Remove support for `username:password@` credentials in URLs. These are deprecated in modern browsers and used almost exclusively for phishing.
3. Remove support for a reject URL. If a user rejects a request, a reject URL allows the user to still be phished.
4. Add a "Copy" button to the generated application password after approval.

I've been working on these enhancements in https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/11079.

Any further suggested improvements should go into separate tickets.

Related: #62064

summary: Send email notification when an application password is added
_description:
When the account password or email address of a user is changed (either by the user themselves or by an administrator) an email gets sent to the email address of the user informing them of the change. This email helps prevent a user account takeover from going unnoticed.

No such email is sent when an application password is added to a user's account. An application password is almost as privileged as the user's main password as it can be used to perform actions via the REST API, even though it can't be used to log in to wp-admin.

An email should be sent to the user when an application password is added to their account. If the creation of the application password is unexpected then this informs the user about it.

Web services such as GitHub send an email to a user informing them about newly granted access to their account for third party apps. The wording of the email sent by WordPress could be similar, framing it as an app now having access via a newly created application password. One important difference is that the name of the application password is controlled by the user adding the password, unlike services where a third party app is prohibited from using a name that might imply that it's a first party connection. If an attacker adds an application password with the name "WordPress" or the name of the site itself, it would be confusing for the user to receive an email which says "WordPress now has access to your user account".

That's a long way of saying that we need to be careful of how this email is phrased.

Abilities API: Add a fast site health summary to `core/get-environment-info`
_description:
Extend `core/get-environment-info` with two additive changes:

 1. An optional `fields` input parameter that filters the response (mirroring `core/get-site-info`).
 2. A new `site_health` output field returning a high-level, LLM-friendly Site Health overview — "is everything working, what to improve, what is broken" — populated entirely from cached data.

== Background ==

`core/get-environment-info` shipped in 6.9 as part of the orientation layer for AI agents. Adding a cached Site Health summary lets agents answer "is anything on fire?" in the same call they already make for runtime context, without paying for a synchronous test run.

Related discussion: [https://github.com/WordPress/ai/issues/40 WordPress/ai#40].

== Proposed shape ==

{{{#!json
{
  "environment": "production",
  "php_version": "8.2.10",
  "db_server_info": "mysql 8.0.35",
  "wp_version": "7.1.0",
  "site_health": {
    "status": "recommended",
    "counts": { "good": 12, "recommended": 3, "critical": 0 },
    "issues": [
      {
        "label": "Background updates are not working as expected.",
        "severity": "recommended",
        "recommendation": "Contact your hosting provider to ensure WP-Cron can run."
      }
    ],
    "truncated": false
  }
}
}}}

== Behavioral rules ==

 * '''Read cache only.''' Populate `site_health` from WordPress's cached Site Health results — the same cache the admin dashboard widget reads. Never trigger a synchronous test run from this ability.
 * '''Unknown when uncached.''' If no cached results exist, return `status: "unknown"` with empty `counts` and `issues`, so the agent can distinguish "no data" from "clean bill of health".
 * '''Only actionable issues listed.''' `counts` covers all severities; `issues` includes only `recommended` and `critical` entries.
 * '''Bounded payload.''' Cap the `issues` list at 10 entries with `truncated: true` when exceeded.
 * '''Included by default.''' Omitting `fields` returns all properties including `site_health`, matching `core/get-site-info`. Passing `fields: ["php_version"]` filters down to just that property.

Capability check unchanged: the existing `manage_options` gate on `core/get-environment-info` covers Site Health access.

== Open question ==

`core/get-environment-info` declares `idempotent: true`. The `site_health` field can vary across calls as the cache refreshes. The annotation remains accurate in the "no state change" sense but the response is not byte-stable. Worth documenting in the field description so adapters can communicate the nuance.

== Acceptance criteria ==

 * `core/get-environment-info` accepts an optional `fields` input parameter that filters the response.
 * When `fields` is omitted, the response includes all properties — the existing 6.9 fields plus `site_health`.
 * `site_health` reads cached Site Health results only; no synchronous test execution under any input.
 * JSON Schema documents the new field with `title` and `description` on each sub-property so adapters can surface them to agents.
 * Unit tests cover: `fields` filtering, `site_health` with cached results, `site_health` with no cache, bounded `issues` list with `truncated: true`, and confirmation that no synchronous evaluation is triggered.
 * Documentation updated on the Abilities API reference pages (separate task).

Introduce WHATWG-compliant encoding name canonicalization.
_description:
WordPress largely treats character encoding names in an agnostic fashion, passing them off to browsers, `iconv()`, and `mb_convert_encoding()` transparently. This can lead to confusing data flow for text data, particularly because it’s unclear how arbitrary text coming into WordPress will be handled.

The [https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/ ENCODING spec] defines which character encodings should be supported by web-integrating systems and which variations of each encoding’s name should be treated as equivalent aliases.

For example, while `l1` and `us-ascii` are both treated by browsers as `windows-1252`, they are never recognized as such within WordPress. In fact, since `mb_convert_encoding()` and `iconv()` don’t follow this interoperability standard, they fail for a number of supported encodings.

As WordPress moves towards deprecating non-UTF-8 support (#62172), it should provide robust mechanisms for converting text at the boundaries of input and output to aid this transition.

Prior work normalized UTF-8 detection in #61182, but focused on the detection of `UTF-8` specifically, and without taking into account the additional encodings in the WHATWG standard.

Further work should provide standards-compliant canonicalization while being explicit which set of supported charsets is being detected. For instance, the set of `mysql` charset names is disjoint from the set of web standard charset names.

=== Activities requiring ENCODING support.

 - Decoding full HTML documents.
 - Reading and writing emails.
 - Printing `<meta charset>` tags.
 - Inferring MIME content type.

== Related work

 - #64427 inferring MIME content type.

summary: Support for the SameSite cookie attribute
_description:
IETF's [https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-west-first-party-cookies Same-site Cookies draft] was [https://www.chromestatus.com/feature/4672634709082112 shipped in Chrome 51 and Opera 39].

The SameSite cookie attribute instructs a browser not to send that cookie with cross-origin third-party requests (such as iframes, embedded images, and Ajax requests). This effectively mitigates CSRF attacks as, for example, the user will not be authenticated for a given third party URL that's being used in a CSRF attack.

More information on the SameSite attribute can be found here: http://www.sjoerdlangkemper.nl/2016/04/14/preventing-csrf-with-samesite-cookie-attribute/

We should investigate whether setting the `SameSite=lax` attribute is of benefit to the `auth` and/or `logged_in` cookies in WordPress, and if so consider implementing it once the draft becomes an RFC.

PHP uses the `setcookie()` wrapper for setting cookies, which means that setting the SameSite attribute is not possible using that function, until such point that support for the attribute gets added. If WordPress were to implement the SameSite attribute, we'd need our own cookie handling function which constructs and sets the `Set-Cookie` header itself, and use it in place of `setcookie()` (side note: this may also be beneficial to unit testing).

summary: Taxonomy: Add description to the fields searched by WP_Term_Query / admin term search
_description:
`WP_Term_Query::get_search_sql()` hardcodes its `search` matching to
just two columns:

{{{
return $wpdb->prepare( '((t.name LIKE %s) OR (t.slug LIKE %s))', $like, $like );
}}}

A term's `description` (stored on `wp_term_taxonomy`) is never
considered, even though:

- `wp_term_taxonomy` is already unconditionally `INNER JOIN`ed into
  every term query (it's where `taxonomy`, `parent`, and `count` come
  from too), so no new join is required to reach `description`.
- A `description__like` arg already exists for exact-field LIKE
  matching — it's just never combined with `search`.

Because `edit-tags.php?taxonomy=X` is the single shared admin screen
for every taxonomy (Categories, Tags, Link Categories, and any custom
taxonomy with an admin UI all use the same `WP_Terms_List_Table`
class), this affects all of them identically: searching the admin
term list only matches name/slug, never description, with no way to
opt in short of hooking `terms_clauses` and hand-building a `tt.description
LIKE` clause in a plugin.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Create a category (or tag) with a short, generic name but a
   distinctive description, e.g. name "Misc", description containing
   the word "pineapple".
2. Go to Posts > Categories (or Posts > Tags) in wp-admin.
3. Search for "pineapple".

Expected: the term is found, since "pineapple" appears in its
description.

Actual: no results — only `name`/`slug` are searched.

Suggested fix: add an opt-in `search_columns` query var to
`WP_Term_Query` (accepting `'name'`, `'slug'`, `'description'`;
default empty array, preserving today's name+slug-only behavior for
every existing caller), and have `get_search_sql()` build its `OR`'d
`LIKE` clause from the configured columns instead of the hardcoded
pair — mirroring the existing `user_search_columns` pattern already
used by `WP_User_Query`. `WP_Terms_List_Table::prepare_items()` then
opts in to all three columns for the admin search box (both the
`get_terms()` call and the `wp_count_terms()` pagination count, so the
displayed total stays consistent with the actual results).

Application Passwords Expiration
_description:
As a developer, I want the option to set an "expiration" date on Application Passwords so that they aren't able to be used beyond the period of time that I know they'll be used.

=== Use case

I've been working with Application Passwords as a replacement for session cookies in an isomorphic decoupled website. I am generating them programmatically and treating them almost identically to sessions. Because they behave like sessions, I want them to expire. I'm working around this presently by including an expiration timestamp in the Application Password name.

While this feature request would solve that specific use case, I believe this would be a worthwhile addition to Application Passwords to add an option to make them more secure.

REST API: let the media create endpoint record the attachment an upload was edited from
_description:
''Claude Code drafted this ticket from the Gutenberg change, forwarded along:''

> With client-side media processing, Gutenberg is moving image edits (crop, rotate, flip) from the server `media/<id>/edit` endpoint into the browser: the edit is applied with libvips and the result is uploaded through `POST /wp/v2/media` as a new attachment, the same way the editor has always created edited images. See https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/82362 (fixes https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/82295, where server-side edits strip the gain map from HDR JPEGs).
>
> One thing the `/edit` endpoint does that the upload endpoint cannot is record where the new image came from: it stores a `parent_image` entry (`attachment_id` and the source's relative `file` path) in the new attachment's metadata, copies the source's EXIF `image_meta` for any field the new file lacks, and resets the orientation to 1. Edits made in the browser should relate to their source the same way.
>
> Proposed change: add an optional `parent_image` integer parameter to the media create endpoint. When set, it must reference an existing image attachment the current user can edit (matching the `/edit` permission check), and after the upload the new attachment's metadata gets the same `parent_image` entry and EXIF carry-over that `edit_media_item()` writes. Without the parameter nothing changes.
>
> Related: #65367 (client-side media processing endpoints).

Patch incoming.

summary: Add a copy-to-clipboard action to error messages
_description:
**Background**

Concept originally from @matt's [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/08/04/defensive-data-design/ Defensive Data Design post]:

> Error messages should be how you'd describe it to a friend. And have a copy-to-clipboard next to it, so people can put into search/AI/whatever.

**Problem**

When users encounter an error, their next step is often to search for the message or share it with someone who can help.  Today, this usually requires manually selecting the text, which can be difficult in notices, dialogs, mobile interfaces, or messages containing multiple lines.

A consistent copy action would reduce friction without requiring WordPress to prescribe what the user does with the information afterward.

**Proposed behavior**

Relevant error messages would display a copy icon (e.g. https://wphelpers.dev/icons/copy) adjacent to the message.

Selecting the icon would:
* Copy the complete error message to the clipboard.
* Briefly change the accessible label or status to confirm that the message was copied.
* Preserve error codes and other details that may help diagnose the issue.
* Exclude credentials, tokens, personal information, and other sensitive data.

The visible message and copied text could be identical in most cases.  Where additional diagnostic context is useful, WordPress could copy a structured version containing the message, error code, failed action, and relevant non-sensitive environment details.

**Accessibility**

The control should:
* Be keyboard accessible.
* Include an accessible label such as “Copy error message.”
* Provide a non-visual confirmation when copying succeeds.
* Not rely on the icon alone to communicate its purpose.

summary: Fix duplicate <h1> landmark tags on login and password recovery pages
_description:
An accessibility (a11y) and markup validation issue exists on the core login, forgot password, and registration screens (`wp-login.php`). The page currently generates two separate `<h1>` heading landmarks simultaneously, which violates semantical HTML standards and disrupts document structure for screen reader users.

=== Root Cause Analysis
In `src/wp-login.php`, an `<h1>` tag with the class `.screen-reader-text` is dynamically outputted to act as an accessible text heading representing the active page title (e.g., "Log In"). However, directly below that landmark block, the presentation layout wraps the visible WordPress website branding logo image anchor (`.wp-login-logo`) within a second, nested `<h1>` element. 

=== Proposed Fix
The brand presentation element does not require header hierarchical value. This patch replaces the outer wrapper around the logo anchor link from an `<h1>` element to a fallback semantic block `<div>` tag with `role="presentation"`. 

This safely reduces the heading layer footprint back to a clean, single `<h1>` per view, allowing screen readers to seamlessly announce the actual utility context of the page title without configuration conflicts.

=== Environment Details
- **Affected File:** `src/wp-login.php`
- **Testing Setup:** Local WP (Flywheel dev stack)
- **Repository Branch Target:** trunk / core develop clone
https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14292

summary: Tests: Reduce the cost of the heaviest PHPUnit test classes
_description:
#65887 gave the suite its first published timing data and closed. This ticket is where the follow-up work lives: the classes that cost the most, claimed one at a time.

== What we can measure now ==

 * [63410] publishes six aggregate metrics to CodeVitals after every push to trunk: main suite time, p95 and p99 per-test time, maximum test time, and counts of tests over 500 ms and over 1 s. https://codevitals.run/public/WordPress/wordpress-develop/metrics
 * [63412] annotates any test over one second on pull request and trunk runs, with a summary table naming the slowest tests.

The first two trunk data points on August 31 were 443 s and 330 s for consecutive commits that touched no test, so single points are noise on shared runners. Only a sustained shift means anything. The same two runs counted 32 and 20 tests over one second.

== Where the time is ==

One local run of trunk at 6c0f205fd6 on August 16 (PHP 8.3, MySQL 9.7, Docker, single site) gives the shape. Directional, not authoritative:

 * 30,865 tests in 1,066 classes, 234 s of summed per-test time.
 * '''Half of that time is in 22 classes.''' A quarter is in 7.
 * 61 REST API classes account for 49% of it.

The heaviest classes by summed time, in seconds:

||= sec =||= tests =||= avg =||= class =||
|| 16.3 || 197 || 0.083 || `WP_Test_REST_Attachments_Controller` ||
|| 11.8 || 281 || 0.042 || `WP_Test_REST_Posts_Controller` ||
|| 7.0 || 151 || 0.046 || `WP_Test_REST_Post_Meta_Fields` ||
|| 6.9 || 200 || 0.034 || `WP_Test_REST_Comments_Controller` ||
|| 6.9 || 259 || 0.027 || `Tests_REST_API` ||
|| 6.5 || 359 || 0.018 || `Tests_Media` ||
|| 6.4 || 452 || 0.014 || `Tests_Blocks_registerCoreBlockStyleHandles` ||
|| 5.2 || 129 || 0.041 || `WP_Test_REST_Users_Controller` ||
|| 4.9 || 113 || 0.043 || `Tests_Image_Functions` ||
|| 4.6 || 11 || 0.421 || `Tests_Admin_ExportWp` ||
|| 4.5 || 93 || 0.049 || `Tests_Theme` ||
|| 4.4 || 4,474 || 0.001 || `Tests_WpTokenMap` ||
|| 4.3 || 95 || 0.045 || `WP_Test_REST_Themes_Controller` ||
|| 4.3 || 848 || 0.005 || `Tests_Canonical_PostStatus` ||
|| 3.8 || 100 || 0.038 || `Tests_REST_WpRestUrlDetailsController` ||
|| 3.8 || 129 || 0.030 || `Tests_REST_Server` ||
|| 3.4 || 29 || 0.117 || `Tests_Image_Editor_Imagick` ||
|| 3.2 || 95 || 0.033 || `WP_REST_Global_Styles_Controller_Test` ||
|| 2.7 || 70 || 0.039 || `WP_Test_REST_Tags_Controller` ||
|| 2.6 || 49 || 0.054 || `Tests_REST_WpRestTemplatesController` ||

Two profiles appear, and they need different fixes. `Tests_WpTokenMap` and `Tests_Canonical_PostStatus` are data-provider matrices of cheap tests, so the lever is the size of the matrix. `Tests_Admin_ExportWp` and `Tests_Image_Editor_Imagick` are a few expensive tests, so the lever is fixture and I/O cost inside each one.

== How to work a class ==

 1. Claim it in a comment here, one class at a time.
 2. Measure before: `npm run test:php -- --filter Class_Name`, then read the `time` attributes in `tests/phpunit/build/logs/junit.xml`.
 3. Apply the levers the handbook already documents: hoist immutable fixtures into `wpSetUpBeforeClass()`, share expensive objects across the class, trim provider matrices that exercise identical code paths, and mock file or image work where the assertion does not need the real thing.
 4. Measure after, the same way, and post both numbers on this ticket with the PR.

Guardrails: no assertion is removed to save time, no expected value changes to make a test pass, no timeouts are raised, and a test that protects a specific behavior stays even if it is slow.

Related: #42904, #42278 and #41451 (older performance proposals that can now be evaluated against data), #63026 (the bcrypt precedent), #52645, #65887.

summary: Add a Notes section in the Dashboard Activity widget
_description:
Claude drafted the write-up below after a pass through the existing Notes and Activity widget tickets.

Notes landed in 6.9 with #64096 and have kept growing since: post author notifications in 6.9 (#64204), inline notes anchored to a text selection in 7.1 (#65482), and @mention notifications in 7.1 (#65639). The one place to actually read a note is still the block editor, one post at a time.

So there is no answer anywhere in wp-admin to "where is collaboration happening right now?" A note left on your draft reaches you by email, or it does not reach you at all until you happen to open the post. The Dashboard is where a lot of editors start their day, and the Activity widget already answers the two questions either side of this one - what published recently, and what did visitors say - while staying quiet about the editorial conversation.

== Proposal ==

Add a Notes section to the Activity widget, alongside Publishing Soon, Recently Published and Recent Comments.

 * Unresolved notes only, newest first, capped at 5, matching the other sections.
 * Only notes on posts the current user can `edit_post`, which is the same visibility rule `WP_REST_Comments_Controller` already applies to notes.
 * Each row shows the note author, a short excerpt, the post title and a relative date, linking through to the post editor.
 * The section is omitted entirely when there is nothing to show, so a single author site sees no change.
 * A `dashboard_recent_notes_query_args` filter, mirroring the existing `dashboard_recent_posts_query_args`.

Shape-wise that is a `wp_dashboard_recent_notes()` sibling to `wp_dashboard_recent_comments()` in `wp-admin/includes/dashboard.php`, called from `wp_dashboard_site_activity()`.

== Implementation notes ==

 * `wp_dashboard_recent_comments()` calls `get_comments()` with no `type`, and since 6.9 `WP_Comment_Query` excludes `note` by default (#63999, #64145), so Recent Comments is already clean. Notes need a separate query passing `'type' => 'note'` explicitly.
 * Resolution status lives in the `_wp_note_status` comment meta (`resolved` / `reopen`), registered in `wp_create_initial_comment_meta()`. Filtering down to unresolved means a comment meta query, which is worth measuring before it gets committed to - the Activity widget already carries a query complaint in #64506.
 * Note content can contain `<span class="wp-note-mention user-N">` markup. The excerpt needs to render or strip that sensibly rather than dumping raw HTML into the widget. `wp_get_note_mentioned_user_ids()` (added in 7.1) is the existing parser for it.
 * Limit to post types that actually support notes, ie. `'editor' => array( 'notes' => true )` in supports, the same check `WP_REST_Comments_Controller::check_post_type_supports_notes()` makes.
 * There is no deep link to an individual note yet. The editor registers an `edit-post/collab-history-sidebar` sidebar but no URL parameter opens it on a specific note, so linking to the post editor is the honest first step and anchoring can be a follow up.

== Prior art ==

This ground has been circled before, so worth being explicit about what is different here.

#64377 adds a Notes column to the posts list table (has-patch, PR https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/10611). That answers "does this post have notes?" while you are already browsing posts. A dashboard section answers "is anything waiting for me?" before you go looking. Those feel complementary rather than overlapping, but if only one of the two is wanted, that is worth settling here.

Gutenberg explored a broader version of this in https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/71622 and the closed PR https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/71743, which added a posts list column plus a dedicated editorial comments screen. The design feedback there was that notes are scoped to a block, and increasingly to a text selection, so listing them away from that context risks confusion - and moderation UI in particular does not belong outside the editor.

The proposal here tries to respect that. It is read only, carries no moderation actions, and points back into the editor rather than trying to replace it. That is still the main concern to weigh though, and design input would be welcome before any patch.

== Open questions ==

 * All notes on posts the user can edit, or only notes that @mention them? Mentions are parseable via `wp_get_note_mentioned_user_ids()` but they are not indexed, so "mentions you" cannot be done in SQL without storing something extra.
 * Should replies collapse into their parent thread, or list individually?
 * Should resolved notes appear at all, or only unresolved ones?
 * Does this belong inside the Activity widget, or as its own dashboard widget that users can move and hide?

Related: #64096, #64204, #64377, #64506, #65537, #65639, #37578.

Gutenberg: https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/80015, https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/72184, https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/73273

summary: Lazy load user capabilities in WP_User object
_description:
WP_User object are used throughout WordPress and are loaded on the front end [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/907eb2893f331f5d9cda1f277d3dd3137deb0f50/src/wp-includes/class-wp-query.php#L4715 in WP_Query]. summary: wp_insert_user() allows duplicate email addresses containing an apostrophe
_description:
== Description ==

`wp_insert_user()` runs `pre_user_email`, which includes `wp_filter_kses`. That filter expects slashed input and returns slashed output, so for `o'brien@example.com` the value of `$user_email` at the duplicate check is `o\'brien@example.com`.

`email_exists( $user_email )` then queries for the literal backslashed string, never matches the stored row, and the duplicate check silently passes. The value is unslashed later via `wp_unslash( $compacted )`, so the duplicate is saved with the correct address.

[57711] (#52529) fixed the related comparison on update by slashing `$old_user_data->user_email`, but the `email_exists()` lookup was not changed.

== Steps to reproduce ==

Tested on trunk 7.2-alpha-63166, MariaDB 10.11.

{{{
wp_insert_user( wp_slash( array( 'user_login' => 'a', 'user_pass' => 'x', 'user_email' => "o'brien@example.com" ) ) );
wp_insert_user( wp_slash( array( 'user_login' => 'b', 'user_pass' => 'x', 'user_email' => "o'brien@example.com" ) ) );
// Second call succeeds. With plain@example.com it correctly returns existing_user_email.
}}}

Results with an existing user at `o'brien@example.com`:

||= Path =||= Result =||
|| `wp_insert_user()`, slashed input || duplicate created ||
|| `wp_insert_user()`, unslashed input || duplicate created ||
|| `wp_update_user()` moving another user to that email || allowed ||
|| `POST /wp/v2/users` (admin) || 201, duplicate created ||
|| `register_new_user()` || blocked (own `email_exists()` check) ||
|| `POST /wp/v2/users/me` (subscriber) || blocked (`rest_user_invalid_email`) ||

Front-end registration and self-service profile edits are protected by their own checks, so this needs `create_users` or direct API use. It is a data integrity issue, not a privilege escalation.

== Impact ==

Once duplicates exist, `get_user_by( 'email' )` returns whichever row the database hands back first. Anything keyed on email (password reset by email, login with email, plugins that look users up by email) can then resolve to the wrong account.

== Proposed fix ==

Run the comparison and lookup against the unslashed value, for example `$check_email = wp_unslash( $user_email );` used in both `strcasecmp()` and `email_exists()`. This could also make the slashing of `$old_user_data->user_email` from [57711] unnecessary, which is worth confirming in review.

Tests should cover insert (slashed and unslashed), update to another user's apostrophe email, and REST create, alongside the existing `test_reset_password_with_apostrophe_in_email()`.

summary: Investigate Theme JSON Data Caching Inconsistencies
Plugin dependencies: better messaging or management of plugin active states
_description:
Currently, if a plugin cannot be deleted due to plugin dependencies, it has a single message that shows "Note: This plugin cannot be deactivated or deleted until the plugins that require it are deactivated or deleted."

The message is inaccurate in two ways - you cannot delete a plugin unless the plugins that require it are deleted; deactivating is not sufficient; and it does not reflect the current state of the plugin. Much of the structure of plugin dependencies seems to ignore whether a referenced plugin is active or not.

- It should support the dynamic loading of translations when used in conjunction with dynamic imports (`import()`) to avoid downloading all the translations on page load.
- Ideally, it should download the translations required in the initial page load in parallel to avoid waterfalls on page load.
- Ideally, it should rely only on available PHP and JavaScript APIs, and not require any specific tooling.
- Ideally, the APIs should be as transparent as possible to the developers.

Remove mysql2date() usage from core
_description:
`mysql2date()` was originally meant from processing times as stored by WP in database.

Unfortunately its design is very limited because both time zone of input and output is ambiguous. It is interchangeably used for local and UTC times.

As implementation detail that meant that it would produce incorrect output for formats including time zones for local time inputs. Time zone would happen be UTC from WP core setting PHP time zone to UTC on load.

In 5.3 release this behavior was flipped to produce correct local time output for local time input, as considerably more common. Accordingly now ''UTC'' input produces incorrect output for formats with time zone.

While the function is common and familiar, it is hardly irreplaceable and its design is so limited it seems to be unsalvageable.

I propose we move towards eliminating its use in core and eventually formally deprecating it.

summary: Plugin update via modal does not update plugins list until page reload

If you click the "View version ... details" link, a modal dialog box (using an iframe) will be displayed with a button to perform the update.

Before WordPress 6.5, this button was labeled "Install Update Now".  If you clicked the button, the modal would close, the text on the main page would change to "Updating..." and then finally this text would change to "Updated!" when the update was completed.

In WordPress 6.5 and later, the button is labeled "Update Now" (and has a different appearance).  If you click the button, the modal does not close, but the text on the button changes to "Updating..." and then finally "Updated!"  If you close the modal, you will see that the main page has not changed at all: the plugin still displays the old version with the same "There is a new version of [the plugin's name] available..." text.  You have to manually reload the page in order to see that the plugin has been updated to the new version.

Is this behavior intentional?  Probably the change in the button label and appearance was intentional (but that's not very important).  Keeping the modal open during the update might be intentional (although I preferred the old behavior).  But failing to update the main page seems like a bug, or at least a significant regression in functionality compared to earlier versions.

summary: deletePluginSuccess does not update counts for custom plugin_status groups
get_plugins() cache ignores extra_plugin_headers registered after the first scan
_description:
`get_plugins()` stores plugin headers in the `plugins` object cache on the first scan. `get_file_data()` applies `extra_plugin_headers` only while that scan reads files. A later `get_plugins()` hits the cache and never sees headers registered in between.

That first scan often happens during plugin include, before `plugins_loaded`. Any plugin that calls `get_plugins()` there freezes a snapshot with no extra headers. Plugins that register extra headers and then read them get empty values, notices on missing keys, or skip their own update logic.

=== Reproduction ===

1. Plugin A, slug sorting before plugin B, calls `get_plugins()` in the main file (include time).
2. Plugin B adds a header on `extra_plugin_headers` and later calls `get_plugins()`.
3. Plugin B's extra header key is missing from the cached rows.

`get_plugins( '/some-slug' )` is a separate cache slot today, so a folder scan does not reuse a warm all-plugins list and can freeze the same stale headers on its own key.

=== Expected ===

Extra headers registered after the first scan should appear on the next `get_plugins()` call. Already-cached fields (Name, Version, ...) should stay. A folder argument should scan only that folder. `SHORTINIT` should not prime this cache; only `get_plugins()` should fill it.

=== Seen in the wild ===

[https://github.com/sybrew/troy/issues/24 Troy Client #24]. Troy Client registers custom plugin headers and uses them to talk to Troy Server and to keep Troy plugins off wordpress.org's update-check. An early `get_plugins()` meant those headers never landed, so Client could not see its own plugins. Client 1.8.1184 flushes the cache as a workaround. Core should not require that.

WooCommerce has hit the same cache for years. The Helper needs a `Woo:` extra header to see paid extensions (subscriptions and Woo.com updates). `WC tested up to` / `WC requires at least` also vanish, so extensions look untested. Woo already flushes `wp_cache` group `plugins` when those keys are missing (WooCommerce PRs: [https://github.com/woocommerce/woocommerce/pull/26358 #26358], [https://github.com/woocommerce/woocommerce/pull/21669 #21669]). That is a product workaround for this core bug. They knew about the bug, so I'm surprised that they didn't raise an issue with WordPress.

Plugin authors should not have to detect missing keys and flush the `plugins` cache themselves. A core fix does that work once. Sites that update WordPress then see extra headers on the next `get_plugins()` call, so custom update-server connections this cache bug severed start working again without a plugin update.

Themes cannot cause this. They load after `plugins_loaded`.

summary: After uploading a plugin that "requires" other plugins, the "Activate Plugin" button leads to a wp_die() WSOD
_description:
When a plugin is installed by uploading a zip, the result screen always shows an "Activate Plugin" button, even when the plugin's `Requires Plugins` header lists plugins that are not installed or not active. Clicking it takes the user to a bare `wp_die()` white screen with no admin menu and no way forward other than the browser's back button or the "Manage plugins" link.

[[Image()]]

The Plugins list table and the AJAX install flow already block activation in this case (the AJAX flow since #61294). The installer screen should behave the same way.

== Steps to reproduce

1. Create a plugin with this header and zip it:

{{{
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Dep Test Plugin
 * Requires Plugins: classic-editor
 */
}}}

2. Make sure the required plugin (Classic Editor in this example) is not installed on the site
3. Go to Plugins > Add New Plugin > Upload Plugin and install the zip.
4. On the result screen, click "Activate Plugin".

**Actual result:** a `wp_die()` white screen reading "Error: Dep Test Plugin requires 1 plugin to be installed and activated: Classic Editor. Manage plugins."

**Expected result:** the result screen does not offer "Activate Plugin" (or "Network Activate" on multisite) and tells the user which plugins are missing, inside the normal admin screen.

== Cause

Uploads and non-JS installs run through `update.php?action=upload-plugin` and `update.php?action=install-plugin`, which render `Plugin_Installer_Skin`. `Plugin_Installer_Skin::after()` builds the activate links based only on the install result, the `activate_plugin` capability and whether the plugin is already active. It never checks the plugin's requirements, and `update.php` never initializes `WP_Plugin_Dependencies`.

The link goes to `plugins.php?action=activate`, where `activate_plugin()` calls `validate_plugin_requirements()`, gets a `plugin_missing_dependencies` error, and `plugins.php` passes it to `wp_die()`.

== Proposed fix

In `Plugin_Installer_Skin::after()`, when the install succeeded and the user can activate the plugin, call `validate_plugin_requirements()`, the same check `activate_plugin()` runs. If it returns a `WP_Error`, remove the activate and network activate links and show the error message as an admin notice.

`validate_plugin_requirements()` already calls `WP_Plugin_Dependencies::initialize()`, and `Plugin_Upgrader::install()` has already cleared the plugins cache, so the newly installed plugin's header is read correctly. Reusing this function also means the installer screen never offers a link that `activate_plugin()` would reject, including the WordPress and PHP version checks and the `validate_plugin_requirements` filter.

Patch attached.

== Testing instructions

1. Apply the patch.
2. Repeat the steps to reproduce above.
3. Confirm the result screen shows an error notice naming the missing plugin and no "Activate Plugin" button.
4. Upload a plugin without a `Requires Plugins` header and confirm "Activate Plugin" still appears.
5. Optional: repeat on multisite from Network Admin and confirm "Network Activate" is hidden only in the unmet-dependency case.

== Related

* #61294: the same bug in the AJAX install flow, fixed in 6.5.4 by adding a missed `initialize()` call.
* #64493: improving plugin dependency messages (7.2).
* #22316: the original Plugin Dependencies feature, shipped in 6.5.

summary: Twenty Fourteen: Lato font lacks letters for Turkish and other Latin-script languages (requires update)
_description:
Twenty Fourteen has its own copy of the Lato font in `fonts/lato/`. The file `fonts/font-lato.css` loads these font files. The font files are Lato version 1.104 "Western+Polish". These files do not have many letters of Latin-script languages.

== Problem 1: Text shows letters from two fonts ==

When a letter is not in Lato, the browser uses a different font for that letter. The letter then looks heavier, or it has a different shape. Refer to demo.png.

This occurs on sites in these languages. Their translations keep the Lato font on, but Lato 1.104 does not have all their letters:

||= Locale =||= Letters that Lato 1.104 does not have =||
|| sk_SK || `č ď ĺ ľ ň ŕ ť` (and capitals) ||
|| hr || `č đ` (and capitals) ||
|| ro_RO || `ă ș ț` (and capitals) ||
|| hu_HU || `ő ű` (and capitals) ||
|| lv || `ā č ē ģ ī ķ ļ ņ ū` (and capitals) ||
|| lt_LT || `č ė į ų ū` (and capitals) ||
|| vi || `ă đ ơ ư` and the tone marks ||

This also occurs on sites in any language that show names or text in these languages.

== Problem 2: Some languages do not get the theme font ==

The theme has a translatable switch: `_x( 'on', 'Lato font: on or off', 'twentyfourteen' )`. Because of the missing letters, these translations set the switch to `off`:

||= Locale =||= Letters that Lato 1.104 does not have =||
|| tr_TR || `ğ ş İ` (and capitals) ||
|| az || `ə ğ ş İ` (and capitals) ||
|| cs_CZ || `č ď ě ň ř ť ů` (and capitals) ||
|| sl_SI || `č` (and capital) ||
|| bs_BA || `č đ` (and capitals) ||
|| eo || `ĉ ĝ ĥ ĵ ŝ ŭ` (and capitals) ||

Sites in these languages do not load a webfont. The CSS stays `font-family: Lato, sans-serif`, thus each visitor sees a different font:
 * Most visitors see the system font, not Lato. Thus, the design of the theme in these languages is different from the design in other languages.
 * Visitors that have a Lato font on their computer see that font. The result depends on the installed version. On my site (tr_TR), the post titles (weight 300) were very thin. Refer to site-no-webfont.png and site-lato2-webfont.png.

== Proposed fix ==

 1. Replace the font files with Lato version 2.x (latofonts.com, SIL OFL 1.1). Lato 2.015 has all the letters in the two tables above.
 2. Keep the same font family name, font weights (300, 400 and 700, normal and italic, and 900) and file names.
 3. After the update, the translation teams can change the switch back to `on`.

== Evidence ==

 * demo.png: Turkish text in Lato 1.104 (as the theme loads it) and in Lato 2.015.
 * site-no-webfont.png: a post title on a tr_TR site, without a webfont.
 * site-lato2-webfont.png: the same post title with Lato 2.015 as a webfont.
 * The switch values come from the current Twenty Fourteen language packs (api.wordpress.org/translations/themes/1.0/?slug=twentyfourteen).

Related tickets: #29690 (latin-ext subset for Polish), #55985 (self-hosted fonts), #63964 (example of an update to a bundled font).

summary: A request for a Story Editor or Plain Text Editor to make editing invisible text quicker than going to Code Viewer
_description:
I added some custom skip links to bypass some repeated blocks on the website I made, in the process of adding the skip-link classes to a URL, it makes them invisible within the WordPress editor (as they should, since they should only be visible on focus). 
{{{
skip-link screen-reader-text
}}}
The only way to check the text content of that link currently is to use the Link options in the pop-up Editor or go to the Code Editor, which will not necessarily jump to where you are, but you can Ctrl+F those classes to get to where it is. However, not everyone wants to use the Code Editor (I imagine some non-developers might find it intimidating or unnecessarily cluttered). It made me think there could be another way to do this, particularly for invisible text that isn't a link.
What I'm wondering is if there could be a way to integrate into the WordPress Editor a "Plain text preview" mode, where the editor gives the option of previewing as plain text (CSS styles removed), which would also allow any invisible text to become visible again and let you modify the text content as plain text, which would then update in the Editor. 
In InDesign and Scribus there is something like this called a "Story Editor". Those are in a publishing context rather than a website editing context, but I think the idea could have some utility here.
I'm not sure if this would need to be integrated as an entirely new preview mode like "Visual Mode", "Code Viewer", "Story Mode" or "Plain Text Mode", or if it is better to be on a per-block basis, as a "Plain text preview" option on the mini block pop-up editor that appears when you select a block in the WordPress editor (sorry I don't know what this menu is called), or as a Text Content field in the Block Sidebar. If it's a large paragraph that would need editing, a pop up menu might have issues with staying open and editable, so maybe the sidebar or a totally new preview mode would be better.
Just wanted to raise this idea in case other people have thought the same thing. It might be more convenient for quick small edits of skip links or other kinds of styles. At a minimum, you should be able to preview the text in a separate plain text window (to avoid accessibility issues with style conflicts), and modify the text.
**Some resources:** 
[https://helpx.adobe.com/indesign/desktop/add-and-manage-text/add-and-manage-text-frames/open-and-use-story-editor.html Open and use Story Editor (Adobe InDesign)]
[https://wiki.scribus.net/canvas/Working_with_Story_Editor Working with Story Editor]
Note: I realize the first version of this post neglected to mention the Link editor which does have a Plain text type field, but what I'm referring to overall is the ability to view in the editor the text through a separate mode, which could also apply to other blocks like paragraph blocks.

summary: Many PHPUnit tests are not well isolated
_description:
In talking about tests at WCUS 2026, we reminded ourselves that many of our PHPUnit tests leak state and/or depend on previously leaked state. This is easy to see by running the tests in an arbitrary order:

{{{
npm run test:php -- --order-by=random
}}}

This lack of isolation can result in varied problems:
* A test cannot be run by itself
* A test class cannot be run by itself
* A test passes because of some previously leaked state and not because the test is actually testing the correct thing
* etc.

Reducing state leaking reduces fragility, increases confidence that tests are testing what they should be testing, and is a likely prerequisite for future parallel test running.

This ticket is for sharing a grab-bag of unrelated test fixes we worked on during WCUS.

summary: Tests: Let WP_Test_REST_Controller_Testcase reflect read-only routes
_description:
Follow-up to #40538, splitting out the structural half so it can land on its own.

== The problem ==

`WP_Test_REST_Controller_Testcase` declares nine abstract methods (`tests/phpunit/includes/testcase-rest-controller.php`, lines 24–40 on trunk today):

{{{
test_register_routes()   test_context_param()    test_get_items()
test_get_item()          test_create_item()      test_update_item()
test_delete_item()       test_prepare_item()     test_get_item_schema()
}}}

Every controller test must implement all nine. A read-only controller has no create, update or delete route, so those three methods have nothing to assert. Since [53921] and [54058] the accepted way out has been `@doesNotPerformAssertions`, with the note that it "can be reconsidered in the future".

That has not stayed flat. Trunk today carries 101 `@doesNotPerformAssertions` annotations in 26 files, and 98 of them are REST controller tests. Twenty files sit under `tests/phpunit/tests/rest-api/`, plus three under `fonts/font-library/`, two under `icons/`, and one unrelated case in `user/passwordHash.php`. Each new read-only controller inherits the pattern on the day it is written.

== Options ==

 1. '''Default implementations that assert the negative.''' Make the six operation methods non-abstract, with a default that dispatches the operation against the controller's collection and item routes and asserts it is rejected (`rest_no_route`, or the controller's documented error). A controller that supports the operation overrides the method as today. This turns 98 no-ops into real assertions with one change and no per-file work, and it stops the count growing.
 2. '''A read-only base class.''' A second testcase with the read-side methods only, and controllers pick the one that fits. Cleaner signature, but every existing read-only controller test has to move, and nothing stops a future controller extending the wrong one.
 3. '''Leave the abstract alone''' and keep annotating. The status quo.

Option 1 seems the best trade, but the default needs care: some controllers register a route and reject the method with 403 or 405 rather than `rest_no_route`, and the schema for a POST body differs per controller. A first patch could dispatch and accept any error response, then tighten.

Once the base class change lands, the remaining annotations outside the abstract methods are a per-case read, which stays on #40538.

Related: #40538, #41463, #55652, [53921], [54058].

summary: siteurl is missing WordPress path when creating a new site
_description:
Our setup is a single subdomain network. WordPress is installed to `/wp`, and we don't have rewrites configured to mask the subdirectory.

On the initial install, `wp_install()` sets the value of `siteurl`based on `wp_guess_url()`. The main site ends up with these expected values:

* `siteurl`: domain.com/wp
* `home`: domain.com

On subsequent creation of a new site, `install_blog()` incorrectly sets the option values for the new site to:

* `siteurl`: domain.com
* `home`: domain.com

This means the admin loads, but CSS and resources are broken, until I update the `siteurl` option value to be "domain.com/wp".

I'd expect `install_blog()` to follow the same behavior as `wp_install_blog()`.

#23221 is related, although this suggested fix doesn't also fix that.

summary: Users with "same" email address can be accidentally created
_description:
Wordpress does not permit multiple users with the same email address, using RFC 5321 to define the localpart of the address.
However, several major email service providers (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo) ignore mixed case in localparts.
This means that WordPress will support 2 users with email addresses abc@gmail.com and ABc@gmail.com - although those 2 addresses represent the same mailbox.
Propose an enhancement:
  1. Warn admins when manually creating a user that the new email address might be a duplicate of...
  2. Highlight email addresses on the admin Users page that are case-insensitive identical.

summary: Use imageflip() in WP_Image_Editor_GD::flip()
_description:
`WP_Image_Editor_GD::flip()` uses negative dimensions with `imagecopyresampled()`.

With PHP 8.6's bundled GD 2.4.0, this causes `Tests_Image_Editor_GD::test_flip` to fail:


**Failed asserting that 0 is identical to 8434407
**

The same operation works with PHP 8.5/GD 2.3.3. `imageflip()` produces the expected result on both versions.

This patch replaces the `imagecopyresampled()` implementation with `imageflip()` while preserving the existing flip behavior.

KSES: Re-implement using HTML API
_description:
Since its initial commit, WordPress has relied on the KSES library to sanitize and normalize and transform content from untrusted sources. Unfortunately, the parsing inside of `wp_kses()` has never been spec-compliant, leading to numerous challenges in safely, efficiently, and reliably fulfilling its purpose.

The HTML API provides a mechanism for structurally interacting with HTML in an efficient manner, and `wp_kses()` should be rewritten to lean on that existing capability.

== Resolves

 - #25851 Large attribute values may crash PCRE patterns and cause content loss.
 - #37698 Global pollution in `wp_kses_split()` calls.
 - #48873 CSS contents are corrupted by `wp_kses()`.
 - #51482 `wp_kses()` turns SCRIPT and STYLE content into renderable text.
 - #52333 `wp_kses()` and HTML disagree on the set of named character references.
 - #58377 Block names with consecutive hyphens are corrupted.
 - #58921 Valid tag names are rejected from the allow-list.
 - #59310 `parse_blocks()` called unnecessarily.
 - #61246 `wp_kses()` un-comments HTML comments.
 - #62024 `wp_kses_post()` incorrectly escapes “<” in attribute values.

=== Potentially resolves

 - #51093 CSS `>` corruption.
 - #56118 Slashes are improperly stripped when exporting data.

== Related

 - #63881 Deprecate `wp_kses_stripslashes()`.
 - #65599 HTML sanitization API implementation.

summary: New param "allow_multiple_terms" in `register_taxonomy` for single term restriction
_description:
The `register_taxonomy` function is based on the two main taxonomies: categories and tags.

Custom taxonomies can only have those two behaviors: hierarchical terms, like categories or non hierarchical terms like tags.

At this time, when a plugin adds a custom taxonomy, the generated UI is:
- checkboxes for category like taxonomies
- multiple select  for tag like taxonomies

If a plugin needs to exclusive terms, the UI has to be hidden and a custom box added which causes UI inconsistency between plugins.

It would be very useful to natively allow single term behavior, just like post-format does.  
In this case, the UI could be a simple **select** or **radio buttons** (preference for select).


I suggest a `allow_multiple_terms` parameter, with default value **true**

Setting it to **false** would make use the simple `<select>` field.

Caveats:
Need to manage: single edit page, quick-edit and bulk-edit.

WP_Comment_Query can generate negative offset in LIMIT clause
_description:
The {{{paged}}} argument in {{{WP_Comment_Query}}} was introduced in #38268

There's a problem with the {{{paged}}} as 0 case.

'''Example:'''

When the {{{paged}}} is 0 and {{{number}}} is 2, {{{WP_Comment_Query}}} generates the LIMIT clause:

{{{ LIMIT -2, 2 }}}

instead of 

{{{ LIMIT 0, 2 }}}

According to the MySQL documentation, the offset in the LIMIT clause shouldn't be negative:

https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/5.7/en/select.html

I think we should handle it in the same way as in {{{WP_Query}}}, where the 0 case is treated as the default, that is 1.

summary: kses filter silently strips allowfullscreen from Vimeo and YouTube iframe embeds on every post save, breaking video playback sitewide
_description:
Every time a WordPress post containing a Vimeo or YouTube iframe embed is saved or updated, the kses filter silently strips the allowfullscreen attribute from the embed code in the database. This causes the embedded video to display a privacy/playback error to all visitors with no warning to the site owner — without my knowledge. I never know how long videos have not been working. This is not acceptable.

Steps to reproduce:

Embed a Vimeo or YouTube video in a post using the standard iframe embed code provided by those platforms
Save the post
Visit the post as a visitor — the video displays: “Because of its privacy settings, this video cannot be played here”
Inspect the post content in the database — allowfullscreen has been silently removed

Why this is a defect:

WordPress’s own embed block and oEmbed system generate iframe code that includes allowfullscreen. The kses filter then strips it on save — meaning WordPress is actively breaking its own output with zero warning to the user.

allowfullscreen is not a security risk. It is a standard HTML5 attribute that permits an iframe to enter fullscreen mode. It poses no cross-site scripting risk, no injection vector, and no security concern of any kind. It has been a standard part of the HTML5 specification since 2012.

Real-world impact:

I have operated a professional WordPress broadcast platform since 2009. Over nearly two decades, I have hosted leaders from every major industry — producing close to 300 episodes of long-form video interviews and 300 audio episodes that serve as a permanent public archive. This is serious, professional publishing work on WordPress.

This issue has been silently breaking professional video publishers like me for over a decade. A site with hundreds of video episodes can have every single video broken simultaneously simply because the site owner edited and saved a post for any reason — fixing a typo, updating metadata, adding a transcript. There is no warning. Visitors see broken videos. The site owner has no idea until a visitor reports it.

I want to be more active on my site — updating content, adding transcripts for accessibility and SEO, improving posts. But every time I save a post, my entire video library breaks. This is not a theoretical edge case. This is a recurring, documented failure that is actively discouraging professional publishers from maintaining and improving their WordPress sites.

My site is itsrainmakingtime.ch — a broadcast platform that has been live on WordPress since 2009.

Requested fix:

Add allowfullscreen to the kses allowed attributes whitelist for iframe elements. This is a one-line fix that would permanently resolve a user-hostile bug that has persisted since 2012.

I respectfully urge the WordPress core team to prioritize this fix. Professional publishers deserve better.

Thank you in advance. 

Kim Greenhouse
itsrainmakingtime.ch
